strengths: Addresses an important problem: fine-grained inference-time control of a frozen text-to-music model without retraining or per-step optimization.
The RFM-to-MusicGen adaptation is intuitively motivated, and the layer weighting, stochastic injection, temporal scheduling, and multi-attribute extensions form a coherent framework.
The evaluation explores several settings, including single- and multi-direction steering, temporal crossfades, synthetic data, preliminary real-music transfer, and a listening study.
The note-steering results are strong according to the paper's probe metric, and the ablations clearly illustrate the trade-off between controllability, distribution shift, and prompt adherence.
The paper acknowledges important limitations, including weak absolute performance on several attributes and questionable generalization of synthetic-data probes.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is substantially circular. RFM-derived directions are steered and then evaluated primarily with separate but closely related RFM probes trained on the same datasets and model representations. Increasing probe scores establishes movement in a probe-preferred direction, but not necessarily that listeners or independent music-analysis systems perceive the intended note, chord, interval, or progression.

The listening study is too small and underspecified to provide convincing independent validation: it uses only 12 participants and three samples per condition, does not define the rating scale, conflates audio quality with control adherence, and omits participant expertise, randomization, statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, and inter-rater reliability.

Comparisons are inadequate. The steering experiments lack simple activation-space baselines such as class-mean differences, linear-probe directions, or CAA-style directions, as well as comparisons with relevant music-control approaches such as activation patching or SMITIN. The reported probe-classification comparison does not establish that RFM directions provide superior steering.

Several essential implementation details are missing or ambiguous, including construction of each class-specific direction, resolution of the arbitrary eigenvector sign, direction normalization, exact residual-stream injection location, dataset sizes and prompts for most experiments, random seeds, and inference-time cost.

Claims of general fine-grained musical control are not supported across attributes. Single-direction accuracies remain very low for progressions, scales, intervals, and time signatures. Temporal control is validated using the same representation-space probe rather than independent frame-level pitch/chord estimators or temporally resolved human judgments.

The multi-direction evaluation reports marginal per-attribute averages aggregated across pairings rather than joint success rates for satisfying both requested attributes. It therefore does not convincingly demonstrate simultaneous control, while its CLAP and distributional metrics degrade substantially.

The MusicBench experiment is preliminary and incomplete: Table 4 appears to report only key steering, despite discussion of notes, keys, and tempo, and provides no baselines, uncertainty, class distribution, or independent verification of the generated musical attributes.

FD and MMD are insufficiently specified—the embedding space, reference distribution, estimator, and sample sizes are unclear—and nearly all quantitative results lack uncertainty estimates. Hyperparameter selection and evaluation also appear insufficiently separated, creating possible selection bias.

The novelty beyond prior RFM steering is mainly a domain adaptation plus heuristic layer weighting, stochastic gating, and schedules. Given the lack of independent validation and competitive baselines, the evidence is not yet strong enough for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: fine-grained control of a frozen text-to-music model without retraining or iterative inference-time optimization.

Adapting RFM-derived directions to MusicGen is technically plausible, and the combination of layer selection, stochastic injection, temporal schedules, and multi-attribute steering provides a flexible framework.

The experiments cover synthetic and real-music data, probe performance, single- and multi-direction steering, temporal control, ablations, and a small listening study. The paper also acknowledges weaknesses of synthetic-data probes and mean pooling.
The note-steering results are promising, with probe accuracy increasing substantially as steering strength grows.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is partly circular. Steering directions and the main concept-accuracy evaluator are both RFM probes trained on the same representations and concept data. Increased probe scores establish movement in a probe-defined direction, but do not independently demonstrate that the rendered audio contains the intended note, chord, interval, or temporal structure. Standard transcription, chord/key estimation, symbolic analysis, or a sufficiently rigorous listening study is needed.

The listening study is far too underspecified and small to resolve this concern: only 12 participants and apparently three clips per control type are used, while the rating scale, participant expertise, assignment design, blinding, randomization, separate quality/control questions, confidence intervals, and significance tests are not reported. The displayed standard deviations do not establish statistically reliable superiority.

There are no competitive steering baselines such as activation addition/contrastive activation addition, activation patching, or relevant music intervention methods. Comparisons are mainly against no steering and the authors' own naive RFM variant, so the experiments do not show that RFM directions are preferable to simpler activation directions.

A key technical detail is missing: AGOP eigenvectors have arbitrary sign, yet the paper does not explain how each binary direction is oriented so that positive injection steers toward the target class. It is also unclear how directions learned after recursive feature transformations are mapped consistently back into the original residual-stream coordinates. These omissions impair both soundness assessment and reproducibility.

Claims of broadly effective fine-grained control are stronger than the results. Outside notes, absolute probe accuracies are often low and improve only modestly; temporal results again measure the same probe's internal probability rather than independently verified musical events. Multi-direction steering severely worsens FD/MMD and CLAP, so it does not convincingly preserve generation quality or prompt adherence.

The real-music evaluation is incomplete and ambiguously positioned. New probes are fitted directly on MusicBench rather than demonstrating transfer of Syntheory-trained directions, Table 4 reports only key steering, and it lacks an unsteered baseline. This does not substantiate the claimed generalization across real-music attributes.

Important experimental details are absent, including sample counts for several main tables, prompt and reference-set construction, audio duration, FD/MMD embedding definitions, repeated-run variability, random seeds, and statistical uncertainty. Probe comparison fairness is also unclear because the Syntheory FFN results are imported while MusicRFM receives extensive hyperparameter search and an insufficiently described aggregation model.

The novelty is moderate: RFM-based activation steering already exists, while top-K layer selection, score weighting, schedules, Bernoulli gating, and vector addition are relatively standard extensions. Given the missing independent validation and strong baselines, the current evidence is not competitive for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting application of Recursive Feature Machines to inference-time control of a frozen MusicGen model, avoiding base-model fine-tuning and per-step optimization.
Layer selection, stochastic injection, time-varying schedules, crossfading, and multi-attribute steering form a flexible and practically relevant control framework.

The experiments cover several music-theoretic attributes, include preliminary transfer to real music, and clearly expose the trade-off between control strength, distributional drift, and prompt adherence.
The layer-weighting, top-K, pooling, and injection-probability ablations provide useful empirical insight, and the paper candidly discusses several limitations.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation is partly circular: directions derived from RFM probes are judged using closely related RFM probes. Rising probe scores—and especially schedule-shaped probe traces—do not independently establish that the resulting audio contains the intended musical property. Independent transcription, beat/key/chord estimators, or expert annotations are needed.

Comparisons are inadequate for supporting the paper's practical contribution. Steering is compared mainly with no steering and the authors' own naive RFM variant, rather than activation addition, activation patching, SMITIN, or representative controllable music-generation methods under matched conditions.

The listening study is too small and underspecified: it uses only 12 participants and apparently three clips per condition, with no rating-scale definition, randomization details, participant expertise, significance tests, confidence intervals, or inter-rater analysis. Consequently, it offers weak support for claims about perceptual quality and control.

Effectiveness is highly uneven. Strong control is demonstrated primarily for notes; chord, interval, scale, progression, and time-signature accuracies remain low. Multi-direction steering substantially degrades CLAP and distributional metrics, so the broad claims of fine-grained control with minimal loss of fidelity are stronger than the evidence.

The real-music evaluation is preliminary and unclear: Table 4 reports only key steering despite discussion of notes and tempo, and its accuracy again appears probe-based. This does not convincingly demonstrate transfer to natural music.

Important reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous, including how eigenvector signs and target-specific directions are selected, generation counts for several experiments, definitions and feature spaces for FD/MMD, reference sets, random-seed variability, computational cost, and statistical uncertainty. Extensive hyperparameter search also makes the comparison with previously reported probe results difficult to interpret fairly.

strengths: The paper presents a practically appealing approach for controlling a frozen autoregressive music model without fine-tuning or decoding-time optimization.
The study covers several useful control settings, including layer selection, stochastic injection, time-varying schedules, and simultaneous multi-attribute steering.
The note-control results are promising: target-note dominance increases substantially with steering strength, and an external chromagram-based evaluator partly corroborates the probe-based results.
The paper includes quantitative ablations, evaluation on both synthetic and real-music datasets, and a small listening study, making the empirical scope broader than a minimal proof of concept.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation is circular: RFM-derived directions are evaluated using closely related RFM probes trained on the same concept formulation. A steered hidden state can receive a high probe score without the decoded audio actually exhibiting the attribute. Independent waveform evaluators are provided only for notes, chords, and tempo, and their gains are much weaker for chords; intervals, scales, progressions, time signatures, multi-direction control, and temporal control lack independent validation.

The temporal-control evidence is particularly insufficient. The curves are obtained by applying a probe trained on mean-pooled clip representations to individual generation-step states, which are out of distribution for that probe. Moreover, these internal scores may directly reflect the injected vector. Time-local chromagram, chord, or onset analyses of the generated waveform are needed to establish audible temporal control.

Baselines are inadequate for the central methodological claim. The main comparison is prompt engineering, with no comparison against activation addition, contrastive activation addition, activation patching, SMITIN, linear-probe directions, mean-difference vectors, or random/PCA directions. Consequently, the experiments do not show that the RFM construction is necessary or better than simpler activation-steering approaches.

Important technical details are underspecified. An AGOP eigenvector has arbitrary sign, yet the paper does not explain how its sign is calibrated to increase a target attribute. The construction and selection of class-specific binary directions, activation normalization, exact hook location, and direction selection are also unclear. The pseudocode appears to sample a Bernoulli gate separately inside each layer, whereas the method defines a common per-timestep gate.

The listening study is too small and weakly designed to support perceptual-quality claims: it has only 12 participants and a small randomly selected clip set, combines quality and control adherence into an unclear score, and reports no blinding procedure, statistical tests, confidence intervals, or separate ratings for fidelity and control.

Results lack uncertainty across generation seeds, significance tests, and several evaluation details needed for reproducibility, including the precise FD/MMD embedding and estimator, sampling configuration, audio duration, prompt/class sampling, evaluator settings, and computational overhead. The claimed efficiency is not supported by runtime, memory, or probe-training cost measurements.

Several claims overstate the evidence. At the setting where note probe accuracy reaches 0.824, CLAP falls from 0.332 to 0.303, a drop of about 0.03 rather than the approximately 0.02 emphasized in the abstract. Multi-direction steering reduces CLAP much more severely, to roughly 0.13–0.21. The MusicBench experiment retrains RFMs on MusicBench, so it does not demonstrate transfer of directions learned from synthetic data.

The contribution is mainly an adaptation of previously proposed RFM steering plus relatively standard layer weighting and temporal schedules. Without strong activation-steering baselines or independently verified control across the advertised attributes, the novelty and empirical support are insufficient for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: MusicRFM is a practically appealing adaptation of activation-space steering to a frozen MusicGen model, avoiding base-model fine-tuning and per-step optimization.

The paper explores several useful control mechanisms—layer weighting, stochastic injection, temporal schedules, and multiple simultaneous directions—and includes ablations that expose the trade-off between control strength and distributional drift.
The experiments cover synthetic data, a real-music dataset, waveform-based evaluators, and a small listening study. Note steering in particular exhibits substantial and reasonably consistent gains.
The manuscript is generally organized and provides equations, pseudocode, probe-training details, and extensive quantitative tables.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is substantially self-referential. Directions are obtained from RFM probes, while headline control accuracy and temporal behavior are measured using closely related RFM probes trained on the same concepts and representations. Injecting a probe-derived direction and then observing the probe score increase does not independently establish that the audible musical property changed as claimed.

Independent acoustic validation is too limited to resolve this circularity. It covers only notes, chords, and tempo; uses coarse dominance or onset-rate proxies; and omits intervals, scales, progressions, time signatures, multi-attribute joint success, and temporally localized correctness. The reported tempo correlations are also weak (0.283 and 0.433).

The multi-direction experiment reports marginal per-attribute accuracy after pooling across pairings, rather than the fraction of samples satisfying both requested attributes. It therefore does not substantiate the claimed simultaneous enforcement of multiple properties. Likewise, the temporal experiments largely validate schedules through internal probe traces rather than time-localized acoustic or human judgments.

Evidence that audio quality is preserved is insufficient. FD/MMD quantify distributional difference rather than perceptual quality, and CLAP measures text alignment rather than artifacts or fidelity. The listening study has only 12 participants and 24 selected clips, combines quality and control adherence into one score, and reports no significance tests or confidence intervals. The abstract's approximately 0.02 CLAP-loss claim is also optimistic at the setting producing 0.82 note accuracy: 0.303 versus the stated 0.332 baseline is a 0.029 decrease.

The baseline set is not competitive enough. Comparisons are primarily against prompt conditioning and the authors' naïve variant, without empirical comparisons to activation addition/contrastive steering, activation patching, SMITIN, or representative trainable music-control approaches discussed in related work. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that RFM directions are preferable to simpler activation directions.

Important implementation details needed to reproduce or assess the intervention are missing, including how the arbitrary sign of each AGOP eigenvector is oriented toward the positive class, how class-specific directions are selected, activation/direction normalization, decoding parameters, generation duration, random seeds, and the precise aggregation procedure. The layer and injection settings described as optimal appear to have been selected from the reported evaluations, but no separate generation-level development set or nested selection protocol is identified. Combined with extensive probe hyperparameter search and a lack of uncertainty estimates for automated metrics, this raises selection-bias concerns.

The contribution is incremental relative to prior RFM steering: layer selection, deterministic schedules, and summing multiple directions are sensible engineering extensions, but the current evidence does not demonstrate a sufficiently robust or general advance for a top-tier acceptance. Ethical and copyright implications of steering a pretrained music generator are also not discussed.

strengths: MusicRFM presents a useful and intuitive application of RFM-derived activation steering to a frozen autoregressive music model, avoiding base-model fine-tuning and per-step optimization.
The paper goes beyond static single-attribute control by introducing layer selection/weighting, stochastic injection, time-varying schedules, crossfades, and multi-attribute steering.

The experimental section is broad, covering seven musical concept categories, prompt-adherence and distributional metrics, waveform-based evaluators, a listening study, ablations, and a preliminary real-music experiment.
The note-control results are compelling: target-note accuracy and independently measured pitch-class dominance increase substantially and monotonically with steering strength.
The paper is clearly organized, acknowledges important limitations, and provides useful analyses of the trade-off between controllability and generation fidelity.
weaknesses: Much of the central evidence is partly circular: steering directions are derived from RFM probes and success is then measured using closely related RFM probes. This particularly weakens the multi-direction, temporal-schedule, crossfade, and MusicBench claims. Waveform-based validation is provided only for notes, chords, and a tempo proxy.

The temporal experiments show that an RFM probe's score follows the injected schedule, but do not establish that the audible musical attribute follows that schedule. Because the probe was trained on mean-pooled clip representations and is evaluated per timestep, this evaluation also appears distributionally mismatched. Time-local transcription or human annotation is needed.

Baseline coverage is insufficient for the claimed contribution. The main comparison is prompt engineering; there is no controlled comparison with simpler activation directions or relevant inference-time music-steering methods such as activation patching or self-monitored intervention. It is therefore unclear whether RFMs themselves provide a meaningful advantage.

Important methodological details are missing or ambiguous, including how an AGOP eigenvector is associated and oriented toward a particular target class despite eigenvector sign ambiguity, the precise steering-vector selection procedure, generation and sampling settings, and the embeddings/reference sets used for FD and MMD. The stochastic-gating equation uses a shared timestep gate, while the pseudocode samples a gate separately inside each layer.

The listening study is too small and underspecified to provide strong perceptual evidence: it uses 12 participants and a limited set of selected clips, while omitting the exact rating instrument, presentation/randomization and blinding procedures, participant-level analysis, confidence intervals, and statistical significance tests.

The real-music experiment appears to fit new probes on MusicBench rather than demonstrate transfer of directions learned from SYNTHEORY, and steering is again evaluated with the associated probe. Thus it provides only preliminary evidence for generalization to realistic music.

Several broad claims are stronger than the results. At higher steering strengths, CLAP and distributional quality deteriorate sharply, especially for multi-direction control, while several concepts obtain only modest absolute control accuracy. The method is convincingly effective for pitch but less established for chords, intervals, progressions, scales, and time signatures.

The chosen 'optimal' steering configuration appears selected from the reported evaluations, and uncertainty or multi-seed analysis is generally absent. This makes the robustness of metric differences and hyperparameter conclusions difficult to assess.
